video_title: Liaquat Ahamed on Financial Crises, Gold, and the Lessons of 1873
transcript: TYLER COWEN: Hello everyone, and welcome back to  Conversations with Tyler. Today I am chatting with   Liaquat Ahamed, who is the author of a new  and wonderful book, 1873: The Rothschilds,   the First Great Depression, and the Making of  the Modern World, which I enjoyed very much.   Many of you will know him as  the author of Lords of Finance:   The Bankers Who Broke the World, from 2009, a  book that won the Pulitzer Prize for history   and numerous other awards. Liaquat also has  extensive experience in the private sector,   dealing with the World Bank and the IMF, and he  has headed the World Bank’s investment decisions.   He’s also produced a movie about Iraq and  done much more as well. Liaquat, welcome. LIAQUAT AHAMED: Thank you, Tyler. COWEN: I have a general question about how your  work fits together. Your book Lords of Finance,   it convinced me that financial crises  really matter, and your new book, 1873,   almost convinced me that financial crises don’t  really matter, because the world just keeps   on growing. What makes the difference for when,  historically speaking, crises will really matter? AHAMED: I think the first book,  Lords of Finance, was about the   financial crisis that really plunged the world  into a Great Depression. The second, 1873,   is about a crisis that didn’t actually plunge the  world into a terrible great depression, but what   it did was cause a sequence of effects throughout  the world which damaged the political economy of   the world for the next 20 years. A better title  would have been The First Great Deflation. COWEN: We’re supposed to believe that  deflation is bad, nominal wages are sticky.   This was a pretty slow deflation, but by one  measure, the major world economies are growing   2.5 percent over the next 20 years from 1873  onwards. How did we adjust so well to this? AHAMED: Because prices were  flexible. Nominal wages went down.   I think the distributional consequences and  the political impact of those distributional   consequences were much more damaging  than the pure economic consequences. COWEN: In the 1920s, and a  bit afterwards, of course,   you could say politics goes crazy in many  countries, most of all in Europe. After 1873,   would you say politics went crazy, or it  just continued along its 19th-century path? AHAMED: No, I don’t think it went crazy, but it  wasn’t a happy time politically—it’s populism in   the United States, the resurgence of protectionism  in Europe, the retreat from liberal ideas, the   revival of imperialism by Britain when it invaded  Egypt. Those were not happy things that happened. COWEN: I wouldn’t endorse any of those, but  they sound a bit like business as usual for   Europe in the 19th century. England goes many  places in that century, often with bad results,   but Egypt hardly seems like a major outlier,  right? There was protectionism throughout. AHAMED: It was the beginning of  the scramble for Africa and gave   a second wind to imperialism  because you could argue that   until then there was actually a retreat  away from the growth of imperialism. COWEN: Do you view imperialism as  a natural expression of liberalism,   or as something contrary to its spirit?  Because the liberals themselves often   favored it. There’s a whole literature  called liberal imperialism as a topic. AHAMED: No, I think it’s definitely  contrary to the spirit of liberalism. COWEN: The liberalism of that era, surely it was  a doctrine that thought England and some other   countries could improve the rest of the world.  They thought of that as quite a liberal idea.   Malthus and Mill, of course, worked for  the East India Company. They don’t seem so   morally torn over that. I’m not saying they  were correct, but isn’t that in some way a   high watermark of liberalism to think you can  reengineer the whole world along liberal lines? AHAMED: Yes, you’re right. They didn’t think  that they were damaging these societies,   but I think the long-run  consequences weren’t happy. COWEN: If we look at the somewhat fragmentary  data we have, I see that the estimated rate   of per capita economic growth for the United  States over the period you consider it’s below   2 percent. Some sources would estimate 1.7 percent  to 1.8 percent, but this seems to be the time in   American life where just everything is starting to  change. It’s not fully taking off until the 1920s,   but fossil fuels are being mobilized. Some  centerpieces of modern society are being   laid. Am I right to think below 2 percent is  a mistake, and we’re not hedonically measuring   the improvements carefully enough, and the real  rate of growth was, in fact, considerably higher? AHAMED: God, that’s way  outside my expertise. Sorry. COWEN: You’ve read plenty about this period.  You have a sense of life in 1873 and, say,   1896, which is sometimes when the depression  or recession is supposed to have ended. Don’t   you feel that it’s a bigger difference than  just real incomes doubling every 40 years,   which is like a 1.8 percent  rate of growth would imply? AHAMED: Oh, yes. No question that it  truly transformed the United States.   When I talk about the distributional  consequences and the political consequences,   I think the thing that I focused on  was at the beginning of the period,   the Republican Party looked as if it was going  to dominate American political life for a   generation or two. It had the presidency.  It had both houses of Congress. The 1873   depression or crisis and the subsequent  monetary policy decisions set that back. You got the revival of the Democrats in the  South. In the congressional election of 1874,   the Democrats came back. They almost won the  presidency in 1876. You could argue that they   actually did, and only were deprived of  the presidency because of the backroom   deal. That set back Reconstruction.  That was the end of Reconstruction.   It’s not hard to trace a line from there to Jim  Crow. Those were all terrible things, I think. COWEN: As you well know, we built a lot of  railroads over the last 30 years of the 19th   century. There was the boom-bust cycle, but  we got the railroads. We still have them,   in fact. The people who did all that, who extended  the credit, should we just think of them as heroes   and not villains? They’re the good guys in  the story, just like the people today building   AI. Some of them will go broke, whatever.  It’s their money. They’re building stuff. AHAMED: Oh, yes, very much so. As you said, we  had boom-bust cycles. We had three railroad booms   and three busts. We ended up with  a fantastic transportation system   that knitted the country together. No question,   we should think of them as heroes. There  were a few villains along the way, though. COWEN: Sure. The institutions of this  period, like very loosely regulated credit,   if it’s regulated at all, and flexible nominal  wages and prices, due in part to less regulation,   though there might be other reasons, should  we just look back at those and say, “Oh,   that’s better than what we have now?” Is that  the correct conclusion? If you could have a   big thing that you’re calling a depression,  and we just have a lot of steady growth and   lay the ground for some great infrastructure,  wasn’t that just a better set of systems to have? AHAMED: Did we have steady growth? Half the  period from 1873 to 1896 was classified as   recessionary. The growth was very opposite of  steady. It was very unsteady and highly unstable. COWEN: The average growth seems quite  good, especially if one believes,   as you do, that we’re underestimating  true growth over that 30-year period. AHAMED: Yes. No question. I agree. COWEN: Those were just great institutions?  Why shouldn’t we just like them? AHAMED: Well, can we restore flexible prices?  Can we get rid of nominal wage rigidity? COWEN: I could lessen it. I don’t think our  current political system could. I know what   to do. Trade union privileges, minimum  wages, a bunch of other things, right? AHAMED: Yes. COWEN: That’s good, or that’s bad in your view? AHAMED: I don’t think it’s politically feasible. COWEN: Neither do I, but I could do  it. Could you? Tell me the story of   William Gladstone buying so many Egyptian bonds. AHAMED: The story is that when Britain  invaded Egypt in the 1880s, Gladstone had   put 40 percent of his net worth into Egyptian  bonds. He’d accumulated them over a few years,   but he’d progressively put more and  more money into Egyptian bonds until,   at their peak, they were yielding probably  12 percent to 14 percent. He thought this   was a great buy. It proved to be a fantastic  investment because he invaded Egypt. Britain   insisted that the Egyptians pay off their bonds at  par. There was very little restructuring. Anyone   who invested in Egyptian bonds at that point got  100 cents on the dollar or 90 cents on the dollar. The question is, did he take the decision  to insist that Egypt pay back its debt   because of his own personal stake, or did he  just believe in principle that that’s what should   happen? The interesting contrast is with Turkey.  Egypt owed $500 billion to British and French   investors. Turkey owed $1 billion, but because of  the greater geo-strategic significance of Turkey,   they managed to negotiate to have their debt  cut in half, so 50 cents on the dollar. Even   that 50 cents on the dollar was restructured,  so they essentially paid maybe 30 cents on the   dollar. The differential treatment of Egypt  and Turkey suggests that Egypt got a raw deal. COWEN: Could it be Gladstone thought that  insisting on full repayment from Egypt   was optimal, and he bought the bonds  because he knew he would enforce it,   but he wasn’t doing it to be corrupt. He  simply was trading on inside information,   the way you might find today inside  parts of the Trump administration. AHAMED: Yes, probably. I’m sure he thought that it  was the moral thing for Egypt to pay its debts in   full. If he could have insisted that Turkey pay  its debts in full, he would have also insisted   that Turkey pay its debts in full. He just didn’t  have the power. He wasn’t going to invade Turkey.   He needed the Ottoman Empire to remain intact  as a bulwark against Russia. Yes, I think you’re   right that he didn’t invade Egypt in order to  make a lot of money on his bond investments. COWEN: Given how Victorian the Victorians  were, are you surprised that the Egyptian   bonds were yielding 12 percent to 14 percent?  They don’t seem like that risky an investment   if you know Gladstone will back you up and insist  on repayment. I would have bought some. Maybe you   too, right? You’ve managed the portfolio of the  World Bank. Fourteen percent sounds pretty good. AHAMED: Yes, at a time when 14 percent  nominal and goodness knows what real   because prices were falling,  it was a brilliant investment. COWEN: Now, you’ve done a great deal of reading   about this era starting 1873 or even a  bit before. What has surprised you the   most or what views have you revised the  most as a result of all that reading? AHAMED: I think that the downturn, the depression  portion, was not that great. Surprisingly, the   economic growth was surprisingly resilient.  That’s not the most important thing.   The striking thing about this whole period  was the fractured political economy.   Societies were totally divided in a way that they  hadn’t been before. The liberalism, which was at   its high noon during the mid-Victorian period,  took a big retreat. It laid the foundations for   many of the things that afflicted the global  economy in the early part of the 20th century. COWEN: Who, for you, are the “good guys” of this   era? I take it not Gladstone,  not Joseph Chamberlain? AHAMED: Actually, I’m going to disagree that  not Gladstone. I think he wasn’t a bad guy. The   biggest villain in my whole book is Bismarck.  In an attempt to bring France to its knees,   he not only imposed this giant reparation bill  on France, which then disrupted the financial   markets in Europe; he also destroyed what  was actually a very stable monetary system,   which is bimetallism. I’ve never quite understood  why he decided to hit France while it’s down. France was the linchpin of bimetallism, and held  the largest stock of precious metal reserves,   stabilized gold and silver prices throughout the  early part of the 19th century until 1873. By   destroying that system, he, I think, initiated  the deflation, which then had all of the   damaging distributional consequences during  the last 20, 25 years of the 19th century. COWEN: Is bimetallism stable? Doesn’t it tend to  collapse into monometallism? Because over time,   it may be corrected first, but the  actual market values will diverge   from the pegged price, and you end  up with one currency or the other,   which is okay from my point of view. It’s not  really bimetallism in an active sense anymore. AHAMED: Not if you have a stabilizing central  bank. France had successfully stabilized gold and   silver prices throughout the 19th century, even  after you’d had massive expansions in gold supply.   There’s an argument that they could have done it  even with the massive expansions in silver supply.   You’re right. If there’s giant increases  in the supply of one metal versus another,   that will cause bimetallism to collapse,   but there’s no evidence that they couldn’t  have stabilized gold and silver prices. COWEN: Most currency pegs don’t last for  that long. There’s plenty of 20th-century   evidence for that. You might  get lucky they last a while,   but eventually the central bank runs out  of reserves, runs out of credibility. AHAMED: You’re right, eventually. After  the massive expansion of gold supplies,   the bulk, the fronts, and if you’d had  other central banks doing the same thing,   the central banks collectively, I think, could  have stabilized gold and silver prices. They   would have probably stabilized gold and silver  prices through the big increase in the silver   supply of the 1880s and 1890s. They could  have then shifted their holdings into gold.   I think they could have kept the bimetallic  system going for a lot longer than they did. COWEN: Is it correct for me to think  that the South African gold discoveries,   in effect, ended the impetus for bimetallism? AHAMED: Yes. COWEN: How significant were they? AHAMED: They essentially bailed  out the gold standard. Until then,   during the gold drought of the 1870s and 1880s,  it looked as if the gold standard was becoming a   sort of ever-tightening vice on the global money  supply. I think another decade of declining prices   you could have seen the US abandon  the gold standard and move to silver.   I think the South African gold discoveries  essentially saved the gold standard. COWEN: What do you think of symmetallism as an  option? You have two monies, gold and silver, but   you don’t peg them. You just let the prices float.  You deal with the inconvenience of having two   monies. Some medieval systems approximated this.  Could that have worked for the late 19th century? AHAMED: God, you know, I’ve never thought of it.  I think that if the goal is to stabilize prices,   the average price level, I think a  group of central banks stabilizing   and holding reserves in both  metals would have been optimal. COWEN: The countries that were  on silver flat out—Netherlands,   Mexico, Austria—how did they do? How  was just having a silver standard? AHAMED: They devalued. Essentially, India, China,  everyone devalued against the gold standard   currencies. They didn’t face deflation. There was  no deflation in India. There was no deflation in   China, but it meant their currencies were going  down. It would have been hard to think of their   currencies as reserve asset currencies.  If the US had become a silver currency,   I think it would have delayed the development  of the US as a major financial market. COWEN: Say Mexico was not going to  have a reserve currency, anyway,   the Netherlands, from the vantage  point of the 1930s or even ’20s,   the silver standard back then sounds pretty good.  Oh, devalue, get rid of the deflationary pressure. AHAMED: I totally agree. COWEN: Why did we just push out  silver as a money altogether? Do   you blame Britain for that, or who’s the  villain there? Is that Bismarck again? AHAMED: Yes, totally Bismarck. COWEN: Why did he do that? AHAMED: I’ve never quite understood it.  The Germans claimed that they wanted to   emulate Britain, and Britain was on the gold  standard. Because you can have a bimetallic   global system with individual currencies,  individual countries being either on gold   or silver. That was the situation  during, let’s say, 1820 to 1870.   You just need some key countries and key central  banks to stabilize the gold and silver price. COWEN: Bismarck’s a bad guy, Gladstone’s  okay. Who then are the real good guys for you?   The ones you sit down with, have a beer, and say,  “Hey, I’m on your side, let’s plot something.” AHAMED: I don’t think of this system, or I  certainly don’t think of the 19th century   as divided between good guys and bad guys.  Essentially, all of the people in charge   had no clue how the system worked. I can think of  good guys and bad guys in the 1920s and ’30s, but   I’m not sure that I would think of the 1870s to  1890s as divided between good guys and bad guys. COWEN: At least post-1815, the 19th century  seems like it was, by far, and I do mean by far,   the most successful human era ever. It’s  weird not to have good guys, I think. AHAMED: Right. COWEN: I have some questions about the 1920s,   which, of course, you’re also an expert on.  If you had to steelman the British decision   to re-peg the pound at its previous  parity—that’s what, 1926 they did that? AHAMED: Yes. COWEN: How would you steelman that  decision? Is it defensible at all? AHAMED: Is it defensible? COWEN: Because Germany chooses a  lower valuation, and they end up   in a lot of currency trouble. They end up with  a hyperinflation. The record of fiat currency   up to that time was not very good. Although we  know it’s wrong, was it defensible in some way? AHAMED: It was defensible. I think the  problem was could they have fixed it at   a lower price or a higher price for gold?  Could they have gone back and said, “Look,   all prices have gone up by 50 percent because of  the First World War? We need to revalue gold by   50 percent, all collectively, or change  the price of gold.” I think that would   have been a much better decision because  that would have, with the stroke of a pen,   increased the availability of global reserves and  eliminated many of the constraints of the 1920s. COWEN: If Britain had just gone off gold  altogether, and said it’s a fiat currency   world from here on out, would that have worked or  would that have been a global financial crisis? AHAMED: Oh, I think it would have been a global  financial crisis. I think the fear was that   ultimately—and the example of Germany and  France in the immediate post-war period,   with no link to gold—investor confidence  would not have allowed Britain to do that. COWEN: What do you think is the time  in world history where a true fiat   currency order actually becomes  feasible? Is it as late as 1971?   That sounds so strange to me. I somehow  intuitively have the sense, like in 1890,   someone like Sweden could have just done  it. It would have been fine. Is that wrong? AHAMED: I don’t know enough about Sweden. COWEN: But some smaller country. AHAMED: Yes. As long as you had credibility,   as long as there was a belief that you  would not allow the currency to collapse,   people could do it. Could we have had a global  fiat currency system? I think we did after ’45. COWEN: There’s still a tie to gold through the  dollar. Keynes made sure there was. It was weird. AHAMED: It was both. It was  not really a tie to gold.   Witness what happened when they  broke the link with gold in ’71. COWEN: At least for a few decades, there’s a  sense if the US inflates too much to just turn   seigniorage against the world, that the French  or someone else will convert into gold. That   did constrain us somewhat, right? Weren’t the ’50s  and ’60s, pretty good, macroeconomically speaking? AHAMED: Yes. Did it actually  constrain us? I don’t think so. COWEN: Until Nixon, it constrained us, I think.  Now, the German money printing of the ’20s,   why does that get so out of  hand? Germans, of course,   were pretty smart back then. It’s not  seigniorage maximizing to hyperinflate   to the point where people push money around  in wheelbarrows. Why didn’t they just inflate   at 40 percent or 60 percent and try to get  through at that level? Why did it go so crazy? AHAMED: I don’t know. It happened over a very  short period of time. That’s the first thing,   so they lost control. Secondly, were they  deliberately doing it to convince the world that   they couldn’t pay reparations or to convince their  creditors that they couldn’t pay reparations?   I totally agree with you. I think there was,  under any sort of revenue-maximizing strategy,   it didn’t make sense. Yes, I don’t know. The  only plausible explanation is that they said,   look, the only way that we will  get out of paying reparations   is if they realize that it’ll destroy  our financial system, which they did. COWEN: I had Katja Hoyer, the historian,  on the show a while back. She postulated   that Gustav Stresemann was a kind  of hero of the ’20s. His death was   a great tragedy. He’s underrated.  Do you agree with that assessment? AHAMED: Yes, yes. I think it was under  him that we got the appointment of Schacht   as the governor of the central bank. He’s  the one who stabilized the currency, so yes. COWEN: What’s your view on Schacht? Why did  he turn bad? It seemed he was so reasonable,   so smart. Do you think he was always  bad, or he was an opportunist,   or he was pressured, or he thought  he could still do best that way? AHAMED: I think he was an opportunist. He presided  over the German economic miracle of the ’20s   by stabilizing the currency, was never able  to get reparations down to a reasonable level,   but presided over a Germany that got them down at  reasonable levels. Borrowed heavily from the US   and had an economic boom of the late ’20s.  He always thought that the Allied powers   should have done a better job about reducing  reparations, and he was quite bitter about that. I think when the Great Depression hit,  he realized that he did not want to take   the fall for that. That’s why he resigned  and resurfaces later as Hitler’s minister   of the economy and central bank governor. He  presided over a second “economic miracle,” and   it was based on the fact that Germany had no  reserves, world trade had collapsed, and he had   to do the best he could under the circumstances  and devise this remarkable system of essentially   constant controls and import quotas, and managed  to see Germany through the whole rearmament boom. COWEN: What was Montagu Norman’s weirdest belief? AHAMED: I think he claimed that people could   walk through walls. He had some  very weird spiritualist beliefs. COWEN: He was a theosophist,  right? Is that where it comes from? AHAMED: I’m not sure. Yes. I think  he was part of that generation of   the 1920s where they dabbled in all  sorts of esoteric spiritual practices. COWEN: As you know, the 1920s, they’re a  very rich time culturally for much of Europe.   What is it from that period, from  culture, that you feel closest to? AHAMED: Oh, fascinating question. I suppose I’m  not a great modernist in terms of literature,   so I couldn’t say that I love the modernist  novels. I’m not sure the answer to that. I’ve   never really thought about it. I actually  prefer the American novels of the 1920s. COWEN: Like? AHAMED: Fitzgerald, Hemingway,  those, rather than Joyce and Ulysses. COWEN: Why do you think it’s  seen as such a creative period? AHAMED: Because we’d eliminated the sort  of constraints, the Victorian constraints.   And yet there was a much more sort of  a shared belief in what was great art,   great literature. I know literature better than  I know art. We’d eliminated constraints, and yet   there was a sort of shared culture  about what made for great writing. COWEN: Now, there’s a third book you  wrote, which is much less well known,   and much of it deals with your experiences  at the IMF. It’s a shorter book. It’s quite   vertical. I have a few questions from that  book. Here’s a very simple and stupid question.   Given the price of homes in Ireland today and  the fact that it’s so hard to get anything built,   before 2008, did Ireland actually have a housing  bubble, or were those the correct prices? AHAMED: God, you’re taking me back. COWEN: You worked on this, right? AHAMED: I did, although I was  not a staff member of the IMF.   This book came out of a strange idea that you  could write about institutions by embedding   yourself in for a few weeks and essentially  try and describe what these institutions did   from a journalistic point of view. When  I started the book, my approach was,   let’s suppose you are someone whose son has  just got a job at the IMF. You ask your son,   what does the IMF do? This book was designed  to provide an answer to that. That was the   origin of the book. It didn’t do well. It  turns out I’m not a very good journalist. COWEN: It’s a good book. I like it. AHAMED: Okay, great. Then turning back to Ireland,  I don’t think you can judge a mania purely by the   level. I think you can judge a mania by the rate  of change as well. Prices were going up at an   unsustainable rate, people were buying three,  four, five houses. That’s, to me, the sign of   an unstable economic situation. We got that in  the US. We got that in Spain. We got that in   many places in the world. A bubble has both to  do with the level, but also the rate of change. COWEN: Isn’t this a bit like the railroads?  A lot of the railroad companies went under.   We got the railroads built. Ireland  needed to build a lot of homes. They   actually didn’t build enough. People  should have been buying 10, 15 homes,   not just six or seven. They didn’t  have a big enough bubble, ex post. AHAMED: They should have been building  homes. I’m not sure they should have   been trading on existing homes, but maybe  one couldn’t happen without the other. COWEN: Now, as you probably know, Pakistan  has been through what, it’s either 23,   24 IMF bailouts. There’s something wrong  there, right? Okay, it’s a poorly run country,   but there’s a lot of poorly run countries  that don’t go through so many IMF bailouts.   If we make you dictator of the  IMF, what would you do differently? AHAMED: I would not respond to pressure from the  US to put money into unsustainable countries. It’s   happened time and time again. The US has used the  IMF as a vehicle for foreign policy objectives   which essentially distort the IMF’s  very reasonable economic practices. COWEN: The eurozone crisis, what  should we have done differently? AHAMED: The optimal thing when people borrow  too much is to find a way to restructure   their debts. Now, I don’t remember all  of the details, but it seems to me that   that should have happened. I don’t remember  quite how that eventually happened, but that,   it seems to me, is the flaw in the eurozone  crisis. That was the flaw in the US housing   bubble problem. That whole era was we had too  much debt by people who couldn’t pay it back.   We should have found a better way  to have restructured those debts. COWEN: Was the problem that Europe  had no distributional mechanism for   allocating the costs of that restructuring?  Say they had been more liberal with Greece,   treated it as Gladstone had treated Turkey, but  then which country exactly picks up which part   of that bill? Is that the thing that hadn’t  been solved, or something else went wrong? AHAMED: No, I think that was essentially  the problem. What you need is a sort of,   I don’t know, a hegemon, Germany, taking charge  and deciding how that should have happened. COWEN: Germany was too reluctant  because Germany was Germany? AHAMED: Yes. COWEN: Why does the United Kingdom now seem  economically and politically to be so stuck?   They have a system of government that, at least  on paper, allows for a lot of decisive change,   and yet they cycle through prime ministers  and nothing gets better, and they haven’t   had much real wage or productivity  growth since 2008. What’s gone wrong? AHAMED: God, I wish I knew. I totally subscribe  to the view that things have gone wrong. I really   don’t know because there are so many impressive  things about the UK. One of the striking things   is how many inventors of AI were British.  An educational system that can throw up that   many innovative thinkers and yet not be able to  capitalize on it, there’s something wrong there. COWEN: What’s a part of the world you’re  especially optimistic about right now? AHAMED: Oh, I’m generally optimistic about  most of the world. I’m not very optimistic   about India because of the environmental  damage and because of the water problems   and the inability of the authorities to deal  with that. I’m optimistic about the US just   because I think we will see ourselves through  this downturn in our political fortunes and   the inherent innovation that is coming out  of the United States will see us through. I think that Europe, I don’t know—and I haven’t  been to Europe for five years apart from passing   through. I haven’t spent enough time there,  but I’ve always admired France, for example.   It seems to have hit upon an equilibrium  where people like the balance between work   and leisure and a lifestyle that works very  well. It’s a remarkably innovative country.   I think it probably has more startups  than most other countries in Europe. COWEN: You’re a workaholic, right? AHAMED: No, I’m not. COWEN: You’ve been very successful in the  private sector. You’ve produced a movie.   You’ve written two extremely notable  books. You’re well known world over.   You have the Pulitzer Prize, and you’re  talking to me about work-leisure balance? AHAMED: Well, it’s just I don’t like golf. COWEN: What is it you see yourself as maximizing?  You left Harvard. You didn’t finish a PhD,   which I can very well understand,  but later in life, you come back,   you write these two books when you’re not needing  them for the income. What are you pursuing? AHAMED: An interesting life. COWEN: What makes what you do interesting? AHAMED: I don’t know. Intellectual  stimulation. I’m not a great athlete,   but ideas stimulate me. When you want to find  out about something, writing a book about it   is a remarkably good way of learning it. That’s  what I’m trying to maximize to stave off dementia. COWEN: David Halberstam’s The Best and the  Brightest. Why do you find that book so notable? AHAMED: Oh, it was probably the first  book I read when I came to the United   States in ’74. I find it’s just remarkable  how it opened up the US political system.   I learned so much about how the United  States worked just by reading that book. COWEN: GPT said about you, “Think tanks are  your hobby.” What might it have meant by that? AHAMED: Oh, for a while, I used to kid around  that when I retired from the investment business,   and I was writing Lords of Finance, I joined the  boards of several think tanks. I found it quite   fascinating because these are organizations  that didn’t seem to have the dysfunction of   universities where people were paid and got  a stipend to be able to come up with good   ideas. Being on the board of them exposed  you to some wonderful thinkers. I suppose   I became disillusioned after a point. In part  because these were almost all policy ideas,   and policy seemed to have nothing to do with good  ideas. I suppose 2016 was the turning point in my   mind. That since then, for the last 10 years,  so little policy is driven by great ideas. COWEN: If old-style think tanks are somewhat  obsolete, what should we replace them with? AHAMED: God, I don’t know. I wish I knew. It’s  maybe a model which was less top-down driven.   A model that essentially was more  allowing a thousand flowers to bloom   and create institutions where you allow  people, you get great writers and thinkers   to write about subjects they’re interested  in, and then see what rises to the surface. COWEN: You produced a movie called The Situation,   and it’s set in Iraq. Why did you do that?  This gets back to what do you optimize. AHAMED: No, I had a friend who was a director.  We were talking about the situation in Iraq. It   was more and more depressing. This was in 2003,  2004, after we’d invaded. We’d met a journalist   who’d been stationed there. We approached her  about writing the script. It was a fun project.   It was a total failure financially, so I would  not do it again, but it was a fascinating project. COWEN: Do you follow how Iraq is doing these days? AHAMED: A little bit. I’ve got a couple  of Iraqi friends. Yes, yes, a little bit. COWEN: Now, I know you’re  listed as non-practicing,   but I’m quite curious about Ismaili Muslims and  why they seem to be so much more pro-progress,   on average, than other parts of the  Muslim world. Do you have a view on this? AHAMED: Yes, very much so, because of our  leadership. We Ismailis believe in the   leadership of a man, the Aga Khan. We believe he’s  the direct descendant of the Prophet Muhammad,   and he sets the agenda for the whole  community. Many, in the old days,   people believed he was divine or he had divine  spirit. I don’t think many people believe that   anymore, but he’s invested with so much moral  authority that if he says, move to Africa,   big chunks of the community will do that. He  has charted an incredibly enlightened direction   for the community. It’s not very large. There are  maybe two or three million Ismailis in the world. COWEN: You think it’s that the Imam is nonhidden   that’s useful because he’s  a source of ongoing change? AHAMED: Yes. That was the  whole rationale for Shiism. COWEN: Why is it so persecuted by the mainstream  in Iran? Because it’s a threat to the Ayatollahs? AHAMED: I don’t actually know how many remain  in Iran. It was a very important community in   Iran in the 19th century. The Aga Khan, in fact,  came from Iran and moved to India. The British   sponsored him and invested him with the title  "his highness,” making him, putting him on a   par with other Indian princes. I think there were  probably 20,000 or 30,000 Ismailis left in Iran   in the latter days of the Shah of Iran. I  don’t even know how many remain there now. COWEN: Maybe this is a naive question, but  given that the Ismailis are so successful,   why aren’t there more of them? You’re allowed  to convert, right? There’s no barrier to entry. AHAMED: No. Right. All religions  have some strange beliefs. Perhaps   believing in the potential divinity of a  man is not something that people believe in. COWEN: Some number of Christians  seem okay with that postulate, right? AHAMED: Well, not someone who’s alive. COWEN: That’s a little harder, but  he was alive at some point in time. AHAMED: Well, there weren’t that  many Christians in those days. COWEN: Sure. AHAMED: They believed it  retrospectively after he was crucified. COWEN: Very last question—really  combining two questions. What is   it you want to learn about next,  and what is it you want to do next? AHAMED: Oh, okay. I’ve been reading a great book   about the intellectual movement in  France during the ’40s, ’50s, ’60s. COWEN: The Eakin book. AHAMED: Yes. I find that so fascinating.  That’s what I’m reading at the moment.   What do I want to do next? I would like to  write another book. It probably is going to   be a book about some aspect of the global  economy. I would like to find a subject that   draws on what I’ve been doing up to now, which is  the interaction among countries with a few central   characters as driving the story. A narrative about  the global economy. I thought initially, or the   one that I’ve stumbled across is the ’71 collapse  of Bretton Woods. I’m not sure that has enough   broad appeal, but that sort of checks many of  the boxes of the things that I find fascinating. COWEN: I hope you do that topic.  Liaquat Ahamed, thank you very much. AHAMED: Thank you, Tyler. You took me  in directions that I did not expect. COWEN: Always the case. Thanks.

transcript_segments.text: TYLER COWEN: Hello everyone, and welcome back to  Conversations with Tyler. Today I am chatting with
Liaquat Ahamed, who is the author of a new  and wonderful book, 1873: The Rothschilds,
the First Great Depression, and the Making of  the Modern World, which I enjoyed very much.
Many of you will know him as  the author of Lords of Finance:
The Bankers Who Broke the World, from 2009, a  book that won the Pulitzer Prize for history
and numerous other awards. Liaquat also has  extensive experience in the private sector,
dealing with the World Bank and the IMF, and he  has headed the World Bank’s investment decisions.
He’s also produced a movie about Iraq and  done much more as well. Liaquat, welcome.
LIAQUAT AHAMED: Thank you, Tyler.
COWEN: I have a general question about how your  work fits together. Your book Lords of Finance,
it convinced me that financial crises  really matter, and your new book, 1873,
almost convinced me that financial crises don’t  really matter, because the world just keeps
on growing. What makes the difference for when,  historically speaking, crises will really matter?
AHAMED: I think the first book,  Lords of Finance, was about the
financial crisis that really plunged the world  into a Great Depression. The second, 1873,
is about a crisis that didn’t actually plunge the  world into a terrible great depression, but what
it did was cause a sequence of effects throughout  the world which damaged the political economy of
the world for the next 20 years. A better title  would have been The First Great Deflation.
COWEN: We’re supposed to believe that  deflation is bad, nominal wages are sticky.
This was a pretty slow deflation, but by one  measure, the major world economies are growing
2.5 percent over the next 20 years from 1873  onwards. How did we adjust so well to this?
AHAMED: Because prices were  flexible. Nominal wages went down.
I think the distributional consequences and  the political impact of those distributional
consequences were much more damaging  than the pure economic consequences.
COWEN: In the 1920s, and a  bit afterwards, of course,
you could say politics goes crazy in many  countries, most of all in Europe. After 1873,
would you say politics went crazy, or it  just continued along its 19th-century path?
AHAMED: No, I don’t think it went crazy, but it  wasn’t a happy time politically—it’s populism in
the United States, the resurgence of protectionism  in Europe, the retreat from liberal ideas, the
revival of imperialism by Britain when it invaded  Egypt. Those were not happy things that happened.
COWEN: I wouldn’t endorse any of those, but  they sound a bit like business as usual for
Europe in the 19th century. England goes many  places in that century, often with bad results,
but Egypt hardly seems like a major outlier,  right? There was protectionism throughout.
AHAMED: It was the beginning of  the scramble for Africa and gave
a second wind to imperialism  because you could argue that
until then there was actually a retreat  away from the growth of imperialism.
COWEN: Do you view imperialism as  a natural expression of liberalism,
or as something contrary to its spirit?  Because the liberals themselves often
favored it. There’s a whole literature  called liberal imperialism as a topic.
AHAMED: No, I think it’s definitely  contrary to the spirit of liberalism.
COWEN: The liberalism of that era, surely it was  a doctrine that thought England and some other
countries could improve the rest of the world.  They thought of that as quite a liberal idea.
Malthus and Mill, of course, worked for  the East India Company. They don’t seem so
morally torn over that. I’m not saying they  were correct, but isn’t that in some way a
high watermark of liberalism to think you can  reengineer the whole world along liberal lines?
AHAMED: Yes, you’re right. They didn’t think  that they were damaging these societies,
but I think the long-run  consequences weren’t happy.
COWEN: If we look at the somewhat fragmentary  data we have, I see that the estimated rate
of per capita economic growth for the United  States over the period you consider it’s below
2 percent. Some sources would estimate 1.7 percent  to 1.8 percent, but this seems to be the time in
American life where just everything is starting to  change. It’s not fully taking off until the 1920s,
but fossil fuels are being mobilized. Some  centerpieces of modern society are being
laid. Am I right to think below 2 percent is  a mistake, and we’re not hedonically measuring
the improvements carefully enough, and the real  rate of growth was, in fact, considerably higher?
AHAMED: God, that’s way  outside my expertise. Sorry.
COWEN: You’ve read plenty about this period.  You have a sense of life in 1873 and, say,
1896, which is sometimes when the depression  or recession is supposed to have ended. Don’t
you feel that it’s a bigger difference than  just real incomes doubling every 40 years,
which is like a 1.8 percent  rate of growth would imply?
AHAMED: Oh, yes. No question that it  truly transformed the United States.
When I talk about the distributional  consequences and the political consequences,
I think the thing that I focused on  was at the beginning of the period,
the Republican Party looked as if it was going  to dominate American political life for a
generation or two. It had the presidency.  It had both houses of Congress. The 1873
depression or crisis and the subsequent  monetary policy decisions set that back.
You got the revival of the Democrats in the  South. In the congressional election of 1874,
the Democrats came back. They almost won the  presidency in 1876. You could argue that they
actually did, and only were deprived of  the presidency because of the backroom
deal. That set back Reconstruction.  That was the end of Reconstruction.
It’s not hard to trace a line from there to Jim  Crow. Those were all terrible things, I think.
COWEN: As you well know, we built a lot of  railroads over the last 30 years of the 19th
century. There was the boom-bust cycle, but  we got the railroads. We still have them,
in fact. The people who did all that, who extended  the credit, should we just think of them as heroes
and not villains? They’re the good guys in  the story, just like the people today building
AI. Some of them will go broke, whatever.  It’s their money. They’re building stuff.
AHAMED: Oh, yes, very much so. As you said, we  had boom-bust cycles. We had three railroad booms
and three busts. We ended up with  a fantastic transportation system
that knitted the country together. No question,
we should think of them as heroes. There  were a few villains along the way, though.
COWEN: Sure. The institutions of this  period, like very loosely regulated credit,
if it’s regulated at all, and flexible nominal  wages and prices, due in part to less regulation,
though there might be other reasons, should  we just look back at those and say, “Oh,
that’s better than what we have now?” Is that  the correct conclusion? If you could have a
big thing that you’re calling a depression,  and we just have a lot of steady growth and
lay the ground for some great infrastructure,  wasn’t that just a better set of systems to have?
AHAMED: Did we have steady growth? Half the  period from 1873 to 1896 was classified as
recessionary. The growth was very opposite of  steady. It was very unsteady and highly unstable.
COWEN: The average growth seems quite  good, especially if one believes,
as you do, that we’re underestimating  true growth over that 30-year period.
AHAMED: Yes. No question. I agree.
COWEN: Those were just great institutions?  Why shouldn’t we just like them?
AHAMED: Well, can we restore flexible prices?  Can we get rid of nominal wage rigidity?
COWEN: I could lessen it. I don’t think our  current political system could. I know what
to do. Trade union privileges, minimum  wages, a bunch of other things, right?
AHAMED: Yes.
COWEN: That’s good, or that’s bad in your view?
AHAMED: I don’t think it’s politically feasible.
COWEN: Neither do I, but I could do  it. Could you? Tell me the story of
William Gladstone buying so many Egyptian bonds.
AHAMED: The story is that when Britain  invaded Egypt in the 1880s, Gladstone had
put 40 percent of his net worth into Egyptian  bonds. He’d accumulated them over a few years,
but he’d progressively put more and  more money into Egyptian bonds until,
at their peak, they were yielding probably  12 percent to 14 percent. He thought this
was a great buy. It proved to be a fantastic  investment because he invaded Egypt. Britain
insisted that the Egyptians pay off their bonds at  par. There was very little restructuring. Anyone
who invested in Egyptian bonds at that point got  100 cents on the dollar or 90 cents on the dollar.
The question is, did he take the decision  to insist that Egypt pay back its debt
because of his own personal stake, or did he  just believe in principle that that’s what should
happen? The interesting contrast is with Turkey.  Egypt owed $500 billion to British and French
investors. Turkey owed $1 billion, but because of  the greater geo-strategic significance of Turkey,
they managed to negotiate to have their debt  cut in half, so 50 cents on the dollar. Even
that 50 cents on the dollar was restructured,  so they essentially paid maybe 30 cents on the
dollar. The differential treatment of Egypt  and Turkey suggests that Egypt got a raw deal.
COWEN: Could it be Gladstone thought that  insisting on full repayment from Egypt
was optimal, and he bought the bonds  because he knew he would enforce it,
but he wasn’t doing it to be corrupt. He  simply was trading on inside information,
the way you might find today inside  parts of the Trump administration.
AHAMED: Yes, probably. I’m sure he thought that it  was the moral thing for Egypt to pay its debts in
full. If he could have insisted that Turkey pay  its debts in full, he would have also insisted
that Turkey pay its debts in full. He just didn’t  have the power. He wasn’t going to invade Turkey.
He needed the Ottoman Empire to remain intact  as a bulwark against Russia. Yes, I think you’re
right that he didn’t invade Egypt in order to  make a lot of money on his bond investments.
COWEN: Given how Victorian the Victorians  were, are you surprised that the Egyptian
bonds were yielding 12 percent to 14 percent?  They don’t seem like that risky an investment
if you know Gladstone will back you up and insist  on repayment. I would have bought some. Maybe you
too, right? You’ve managed the portfolio of the  World Bank. Fourteen percent sounds pretty good.
AHAMED: Yes, at a time when 14 percent  nominal and goodness knows what real
because prices were falling,  it was a brilliant investment.
COWEN: Now, you’ve done a great deal of reading
about this era starting 1873 or even a  bit before. What has surprised you the
most or what views have you revised the  most as a result of all that reading?
AHAMED: I think that the downturn, the depression  portion, was not that great. Surprisingly, the
economic growth was surprisingly resilient.  That’s not the most important thing.
The striking thing about this whole period  was the fractured political economy.
Societies were totally divided in a way that they  hadn’t been before. The liberalism, which was at
its high noon during the mid-Victorian period,  took a big retreat. It laid the foundations for
many of the things that afflicted the global  economy in the early part of the 20th century.
COWEN: Who, for you, are the “good guys” of this
era? I take it not Gladstone,  not Joseph Chamberlain?
AHAMED: Actually, I’m going to disagree that  not Gladstone. I think he wasn’t a bad guy. The
biggest villain in my whole book is Bismarck.  In an attempt to bring France to its knees,
he not only imposed this giant reparation bill  on France, which then disrupted the financial
markets in Europe; he also destroyed what  was actually a very stable monetary system,
which is bimetallism. I’ve never quite understood  why he decided to hit France while it’s down.
France was the linchpin of bimetallism, and held  the largest stock of precious metal reserves,
stabilized gold and silver prices throughout the  early part of the 19th century until 1873. By
destroying that system, he, I think, initiated  the deflation, which then had all of the
damaging distributional consequences during  the last 20, 25 years of the 19th century.
COWEN: Is bimetallism stable? Doesn’t it tend to  collapse into monometallism? Because over time,
it may be corrected first, but the  actual market values will diverge
from the pegged price, and you end  up with one currency or the other,
which is okay from my point of view. It’s not  really bimetallism in an active sense anymore.
AHAMED: Not if you have a stabilizing central  bank. France had successfully stabilized gold and
silver prices throughout the 19th century, even  after you’d had massive expansions in gold supply.
There’s an argument that they could have done it  even with the massive expansions in silver supply.
You’re right. If there’s giant increases  in the supply of one metal versus another,
that will cause bimetallism to collapse,
but there’s no evidence that they couldn’t  have stabilized gold and silver prices.
COWEN: Most currency pegs don’t last for  that long. There’s plenty of 20th-century
evidence for that. You might  get lucky they last a while,
but eventually the central bank runs out  of reserves, runs out of credibility.
AHAMED: You’re right, eventually. After  the massive expansion of gold supplies,
the bulk, the fronts, and if you’d had  other central banks doing the same thing,
the central banks collectively, I think, could  have stabilized gold and silver prices. They
would have probably stabilized gold and silver  prices through the big increase in the silver
supply of the 1880s and 1890s. They could  have then shifted their holdings into gold.
I think they could have kept the bimetallic  system going for a lot longer than they did.
COWEN: Is it correct for me to think  that the South African gold discoveries,
in effect, ended the impetus for bimetallism?
AHAMED: Yes.
COWEN: How significant were they?
AHAMED: They essentially bailed  out the gold standard. Until then,
during the gold drought of the 1870s and 1880s,  it looked as if the gold standard was becoming a
sort of ever-tightening vice on the global money  supply. I think another decade of declining prices
you could have seen the US abandon  the gold standard and move to silver.
I think the South African gold discoveries  essentially saved the gold standard.
COWEN: What do you think of symmetallism as an  option? You have two monies, gold and silver, but
you don’t peg them. You just let the prices float.  You deal with the inconvenience of having two
monies. Some medieval systems approximated this.  Could that have worked for the late 19th century?
AHAMED: God, you know, I’ve never thought of it.  I think that if the goal is to stabilize prices,
the average price level, I think a  group of central banks stabilizing
and holding reserves in both  metals would have been optimal.
COWEN: The countries that were  on silver flat out—Netherlands,
Mexico, Austria—how did they do? How  was just having a silver standard?
AHAMED: They devalued. Essentially, India, China,  everyone devalued against the gold standard
currencies. They didn’t face deflation. There was  no deflation in India. There was no deflation in
China, but it meant their currencies were going  down. It would have been hard to think of their
currencies as reserve asset currencies.  If the US had become a silver currency,
I think it would have delayed the development  of the US as a major financial market.
COWEN: Say Mexico was not going to  have a reserve currency, anyway,
the Netherlands, from the vantage  point of the 1930s or even ’20s,
the silver standard back then sounds pretty good.  Oh, devalue, get rid of the deflationary pressure.
AHAMED: I totally agree.
COWEN: Why did we just push out  silver as a money altogether? Do
you blame Britain for that, or who’s the  villain there? Is that Bismarck again?
AHAMED: Yes, totally Bismarck.
COWEN: Why did he do that?
AHAMED: I’ve never quite understood it.  The Germans claimed that they wanted to
emulate Britain, and Britain was on the gold  standard. Because you can have a bimetallic
global system with individual currencies,  individual countries being either on gold
or silver. That was the situation  during, let’s say, 1820 to 1870.
You just need some key countries and key central  banks to stabilize the gold and silver price.
COWEN: Bismarck’s a bad guy, Gladstone’s  okay. Who then are the real good guys for you?
The ones you sit down with, have a beer, and say,  “Hey, I’m on your side, let’s plot something.”
AHAMED: I don’t think of this system, or I  certainly don’t think of the 19th century
as divided between good guys and bad guys.  Essentially, all of the people in charge
had no clue how the system worked. I can think of  good guys and bad guys in the 1920s and ’30s, but
I’m not sure that I would think of the 1870s to  1890s as divided between good guys and bad guys.
COWEN: At least post-1815, the 19th century  seems like it was, by far, and I do mean by far,
the most successful human era ever. It’s  weird not to have good guys, I think.
AHAMED: Right.
COWEN: I have some questions about the 1920s,
which, of course, you’re also an expert on.  If you had to steelman the British decision
to re-peg the pound at its previous  parity—that’s what, 1926 they did that?
AHAMED: Yes.
COWEN: How would you steelman that  decision? Is it defensible at all?
AHAMED: Is it defensible?
COWEN: Because Germany chooses a  lower valuation, and they end up
in a lot of currency trouble. They end up with  a hyperinflation. The record of fiat currency
up to that time was not very good. Although we  know it’s wrong, was it defensible in some way?
AHAMED: It was defensible. I think the  problem was could they have fixed it at
a lower price or a higher price for gold?  Could they have gone back and said, “Look,
all prices have gone up by 50 percent because of  the First World War? We need to revalue gold by
50 percent, all collectively, or change  the price of gold.” I think that would
have been a much better decision because  that would have, with the stroke of a pen,
increased the availability of global reserves and  eliminated many of the constraints of the 1920s.
COWEN: If Britain had just gone off gold  altogether, and said it’s a fiat currency
world from here on out, would that have worked or  would that have been a global financial crisis?
AHAMED: Oh, I think it would have been a global  financial crisis. I think the fear was that
ultimately—and the example of Germany and  France in the immediate post-war period,
with no link to gold—investor confidence  would not have allowed Britain to do that.
COWEN: What do you think is the time  in world history where a true fiat
currency order actually becomes  feasible? Is it as late as 1971?
That sounds so strange to me. I somehow  intuitively have the sense, like in 1890,
someone like Sweden could have just done  it. It would have been fine. Is that wrong?
AHAMED: I don’t know enough about Sweden.
COWEN: But some smaller country.
AHAMED: Yes. As long as you had credibility,
as long as there was a belief that you  would not allow the currency to collapse,
people could do it. Could we have had a global  fiat currency system? I think we did after ’45.
COWEN: There’s still a tie to gold through the  dollar. Keynes made sure there was. It was weird.
AHAMED: It was both. It was  not really a tie to gold.
Witness what happened when they  broke the link with gold in ’71.
COWEN: At least for a few decades, there’s a  sense if the US inflates too much to just turn
seigniorage against the world, that the French  or someone else will convert into gold. That
did constrain us somewhat, right? Weren’t the ’50s  and ’60s, pretty good, macroeconomically speaking?
AHAMED: Yes. Did it actually  constrain us? I don’t think so.
COWEN: Until Nixon, it constrained us, I think.  Now, the German money printing of the ’20s,
why does that get so out of  hand? Germans, of course,
were pretty smart back then. It’s not  seigniorage maximizing to hyperinflate
to the point where people push money around  in wheelbarrows. Why didn’t they just inflate
at 40 percent or 60 percent and try to get  through at that level? Why did it go so crazy?
AHAMED: I don’t know. It happened over a very  short period of time. That’s the first thing,
so they lost control. Secondly, were they  deliberately doing it to convince the world that
they couldn’t pay reparations or to convince their  creditors that they couldn’t pay reparations?
I totally agree with you. I think there was,  under any sort of revenue-maximizing strategy,
it didn’t make sense. Yes, I don’t know. The  only plausible explanation is that they said,
look, the only way that we will  get out of paying reparations
is if they realize that it’ll destroy  our financial system, which they did.
COWEN: I had Katja Hoyer, the historian,  on the show a while back. She postulated
that Gustav Stresemann was a kind  of hero of the ’20s. His death was
a great tragedy. He’s underrated.  Do you agree with that assessment?
AHAMED: Yes, yes. I think it was under  him that we got the appointment of Schacht
as the governor of the central bank. He’s  the one who stabilized the currency, so yes.
COWEN: What’s your view on Schacht? Why did  he turn bad? It seemed he was so reasonable,
so smart. Do you think he was always  bad, or he was an opportunist,
or he was pressured, or he thought  he could still do best that way?
AHAMED: I think he was an opportunist. He presided  over the German economic miracle of the ’20s
by stabilizing the currency, was never able  to get reparations down to a reasonable level,
but presided over a Germany that got them down at  reasonable levels. Borrowed heavily from the US
and had an economic boom of the late ’20s.  He always thought that the Allied powers
should have done a better job about reducing  reparations, and he was quite bitter about that.
I think when the Great Depression hit,  he realized that he did not want to take
the fall for that. That’s why he resigned  and resurfaces later as Hitler’s minister
of the economy and central bank governor. He  presided over a second “economic miracle,” and
it was based on the fact that Germany had no  reserves, world trade had collapsed, and he had
to do the best he could under the circumstances  and devise this remarkable system of essentially
constant controls and import quotas, and managed  to see Germany through the whole rearmament boom.
COWEN: What was Montagu Norman’s weirdest belief?
AHAMED: I think he claimed that people could
walk through walls. He had some  very weird spiritualist beliefs.
COWEN: He was a theosophist,  right? Is that where it comes from?
AHAMED: I’m not sure. Yes. I think  he was part of that generation of
the 1920s where they dabbled in all  sorts of esoteric spiritual practices.
COWEN: As you know, the 1920s, they’re a  very rich time culturally for much of Europe.
What is it from that period, from  culture, that you feel closest to?
AHAMED: Oh, fascinating question. I suppose I’m  not a great modernist in terms of literature,
so I couldn’t say that I love the modernist  novels. I’m not sure the answer to that. I’ve
never really thought about it. I actually  prefer the American novels of the 1920s.
COWEN: Like?
AHAMED: Fitzgerald, Hemingway,  those, rather than Joyce and Ulysses.
COWEN: Why do you think it’s  seen as such a creative period?
AHAMED: Because we’d eliminated the sort  of constraints, the Victorian constraints.
And yet there was a much more sort of  a shared belief in what was great art,
great literature. I know literature better than  I know art. We’d eliminated constraints, and yet
there was a sort of shared culture  about what made for great writing.
COWEN: Now, there’s a third book you  wrote, which is much less well known,
and much of it deals with your experiences  at the IMF. It’s a shorter book. It’s quite
vertical. I have a few questions from that  book. Here’s a very simple and stupid question.
Given the price of homes in Ireland today and  the fact that it’s so hard to get anything built,
before 2008, did Ireland actually have a housing  bubble, or were those the correct prices?
AHAMED: God, you’re taking me back.
COWEN: You worked on this, right?
AHAMED: I did, although I was  not a staff member of the IMF.
This book came out of a strange idea that you  could write about institutions by embedding
yourself in for a few weeks and essentially  try and describe what these institutions did
from a journalistic point of view. When  I started the book, my approach was,
let’s suppose you are someone whose son has  just got a job at the IMF. You ask your son,
what does the IMF do? This book was designed  to provide an answer to that. That was the
origin of the book. It didn’t do well. It  turns out I’m not a very good journalist.
COWEN: It’s a good book. I like it.
AHAMED: Okay, great. Then turning back to Ireland,  I don’t think you can judge a mania purely by the
level. I think you can judge a mania by the rate  of change as well. Prices were going up at an
unsustainable rate, people were buying three,  four, five houses. That’s, to me, the sign of
an unstable economic situation. We got that in  the US. We got that in Spain. We got that in
many places in the world. A bubble has both to  do with the level, but also the rate of change.
COWEN: Isn’t this a bit like the railroads?  A lot of the railroad companies went under.
We got the railroads built. Ireland  needed to build a lot of homes. They
actually didn’t build enough. People  should have been buying 10, 15 homes,
not just six or seven. They didn’t  have a big enough bubble, ex post.
AHAMED: They should have been building  homes. I’m not sure they should have
been trading on existing homes, but maybe  one couldn’t happen without the other.
COWEN: Now, as you probably know, Pakistan  has been through what, it’s either 23,
24 IMF bailouts. There’s something wrong  there, right? Okay, it’s a poorly run country,
but there’s a lot of poorly run countries  that don’t go through so many IMF bailouts.
If we make you dictator of the  IMF, what would you do differently?
AHAMED: I would not respond to pressure from the  US to put money into unsustainable countries. It’s
happened time and time again. The US has used the  IMF as a vehicle for foreign policy objectives
which essentially distort the IMF’s  very reasonable economic practices.
COWEN: The eurozone crisis, what  should we have done differently?
AHAMED: The optimal thing when people borrow  too much is to find a way to restructure
their debts. Now, I don’t remember all  of the details, but it seems to me that
that should have happened. I don’t remember  quite how that eventually happened, but that,
it seems to me, is the flaw in the eurozone  crisis. That was the flaw in the US housing
bubble problem. That whole era was we had too  much debt by people who couldn’t pay it back.
We should have found a better way  to have restructured those debts.
COWEN: Was the problem that Europe  had no distributional mechanism for
allocating the costs of that restructuring?  Say they had been more liberal with Greece,
treated it as Gladstone had treated Turkey, but  then which country exactly picks up which part
of that bill? Is that the thing that hadn’t  been solved, or something else went wrong?
AHAMED: No, I think that was essentially  the problem. What you need is a sort of,
I don’t know, a hegemon, Germany, taking charge  and deciding how that should have happened.
COWEN: Germany was too reluctant  because Germany was Germany?
AHAMED: Yes.
COWEN: Why does the United Kingdom now seem  economically and politically to be so stuck?
They have a system of government that, at least  on paper, allows for a lot of decisive change,
and yet they cycle through prime ministers  and nothing gets better, and they haven’t
had much real wage or productivity  growth since 2008. What’s gone wrong?
AHAMED: God, I wish I knew. I totally subscribe  to the view that things have gone wrong. I really
don’t know because there are so many impressive  things about the UK. One of the striking things
is how many inventors of AI were British.  An educational system that can throw up that
many innovative thinkers and yet not be able to  capitalize on it, there’s something wrong there.
COWEN: What’s a part of the world you’re  especially optimistic about right now?
AHAMED: Oh, I’m generally optimistic about  most of the world. I’m not very optimistic
about India because of the environmental  damage and because of the water problems
and the inability of the authorities to deal  with that. I’m optimistic about the US just
because I think we will see ourselves through  this downturn in our political fortunes and
the inherent innovation that is coming out  of the United States will see us through.
I think that Europe, I don’t know—and I haven’t  been to Europe for five years apart from passing
through. I haven’t spent enough time there,  but I’ve always admired France, for example.
It seems to have hit upon an equilibrium  where people like the balance between work
and leisure and a lifestyle that works very  well. It’s a remarkably innovative country.
I think it probably has more startups  than most other countries in Europe.
COWEN: You’re a workaholic, right?
AHAMED: No, I’m not.
COWEN: You’ve been very successful in the  private sector. You’ve produced a movie.
You’ve written two extremely notable  books. You’re well known world over.
You have the Pulitzer Prize, and you’re  talking to me about work-leisure balance?
AHAMED: Well, it’s just I don’t like golf.
COWEN: What is it you see yourself as maximizing?  You left Harvard. You didn’t finish a PhD,
which I can very well understand,  but later in life, you come back,
you write these two books when you’re not needing  them for the income. What are you pursuing?
AHAMED: An interesting life.
COWEN: What makes what you do interesting?
AHAMED: I don’t know. Intellectual  stimulation. I’m not a great athlete,
but ideas stimulate me. When you want to find  out about something, writing a book about it
is a remarkably good way of learning it. That’s  what I’m trying to maximize to stave off dementia.
COWEN: David Halberstam’s The Best and the  Brightest. Why do you find that book so notable?
AHAMED: Oh, it was probably the first  book I read when I came to the United
States in ’74. I find it’s just remarkable  how it opened up the US political system.
I learned so much about how the United  States worked just by reading that book.
COWEN: GPT said about you, “Think tanks are  your hobby.” What might it have meant by that?
AHAMED: Oh, for a while, I used to kid around  that when I retired from the investment business,
and I was writing Lords of Finance, I joined the  boards of several think tanks. I found it quite
fascinating because these are organizations  that didn’t seem to have the dysfunction of
universities where people were paid and got  a stipend to be able to come up with good
ideas. Being on the board of them exposed  you to some wonderful thinkers. I suppose
I became disillusioned after a point. In part  because these were almost all policy ideas,
and policy seemed to have nothing to do with good  ideas. I suppose 2016 was the turning point in my
mind. That since then, for the last 10 years,  so little policy is driven by great ideas.
COWEN: If old-style think tanks are somewhat  obsolete, what should we replace them with?
AHAMED: God, I don’t know. I wish I knew. It’s  maybe a model which was less top-down driven.
A model that essentially was more  allowing a thousand flowers to bloom
and create institutions where you allow  people, you get great writers and thinkers
to write about subjects they’re interested  in, and then see what rises to the surface.
COWEN: You produced a movie called The Situation,
and it’s set in Iraq. Why did you do that?  This gets back to what do you optimize.
AHAMED: No, I had a friend who was a director.  We were talking about the situation in Iraq. It
was more and more depressing. This was in 2003,  2004, after we’d invaded. We’d met a journalist
who’d been stationed there. We approached her  about writing the script. It was a fun project.
It was a total failure financially, so I would  not do it again, but it was a fascinating project.
COWEN: Do you follow how Iraq is doing these days?
AHAMED: A little bit. I’ve got a couple  of Iraqi friends. Yes, yes, a little bit.
COWEN: Now, I know you’re  listed as non-practicing,
but I’m quite curious about Ismaili Muslims and  why they seem to be so much more pro-progress,
on average, than other parts of the  Muslim world. Do you have a view on this?
AHAMED: Yes, very much so, because of our  leadership. We Ismailis believe in the
leadership of a man, the Aga Khan. We believe he’s  the direct descendant of the Prophet Muhammad,
and he sets the agenda for the whole  community. Many, in the old days,
people believed he was divine or he had divine  spirit. I don’t think many people believe that
anymore, but he’s invested with so much moral  authority that if he says, move to Africa,
big chunks of the community will do that. He  has charted an incredibly enlightened direction
for the community. It’s not very large. There are  maybe two or three million Ismailis in the world.
COWEN: You think it’s that the Imam is nonhidden
that’s useful because he’s  a source of ongoing change?
AHAMED: Yes. That was the  whole rationale for Shiism.
COWEN: Why is it so persecuted by the mainstream  in Iran? Because it’s a threat to the Ayatollahs?
AHAMED: I don’t actually know how many remain  in Iran. It was a very important community in
Iran in the 19th century. The Aga Khan, in fact,  came from Iran and moved to India. The British
sponsored him and invested him with the title  "his highness,” making him, putting him on a
par with other Indian princes. I think there were  probably 20,000 or 30,000 Ismailis left in Iran
in the latter days of the Shah of Iran. I  don’t even know how many remain there now.
COWEN: Maybe this is a naive question, but  given that the Ismailis are so successful,
why aren’t there more of them? You’re allowed  to convert, right? There’s no barrier to entry.
AHAMED: No. Right. All religions  have some strange beliefs. Perhaps
believing in the potential divinity of a  man is not something that people believe in.
COWEN: Some number of Christians  seem okay with that postulate, right?
AHAMED: Well, not someone who’s alive.
COWEN: That’s a little harder, but  he was alive at some point in time.
AHAMED: Well, there weren’t that  many Christians in those days.
COWEN: Sure.
AHAMED: They believed it  retrospectively after he was crucified.
COWEN: Very last question—really  combining two questions. What is
it you want to learn about next,  and what is it you want to do next?
AHAMED: Oh, okay. I’ve been reading a great book
about the intellectual movement in  France during the ’40s, ’50s, ’60s.
COWEN: The Eakin book.
AHAMED: Yes. I find that so fascinating.  That’s what I’m reading at the moment.
What do I want to do next? I would like to  write another book. It probably is going to
be a book about some aspect of the global  economy. I would like to find a subject that
draws on what I’ve been doing up to now, which is  the interaction among countries with a few central
characters as driving the story. A narrative about  the global economy. I thought initially, or the
one that I’ve stumbled across is the ’71 collapse  of Bretton Woods. I’m not sure that has enough
broad appeal, but that sort of checks many of  the boxes of the things that I find fascinating.
COWEN: I hope you do that topic.  Liaquat Ahamed, thank you very much.
AHAMED: Thank you, Tyler. You took me  in directions that I did not expect.
COWEN: Always the case. Thanks.
